course.title: Game Theory
course.description: How rational people choose when their best move depends on what everyone else is doing - dominance, Nash equilibrium, mixed strategies, sequential play, repetition, and real applications like auctions and bargaining. Structure adapted from Open Yale Courses (Yale University, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: A 'game' in game theory is best described as...
options: any activity with a winner and a loser
any situation where each player's best choice depends on what others choose
a contest decided purely by luck
a set of rules with no players
questions.explanation: Game theory studies strategic interdependence - your payoff depends on others' choices too, not just your own. See 'What game theory is'.

questions.prompt: A strategy that gives a player a higher payoff than another strategy no matter what opponents do is called...
questions.explanation: A strictly dominant strategy beats an alternative against every opponent choice.

questions.prompt: A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies in which...
options: every player earns the same payoff
no player can do better by changing only their own strategy
the total payoff is as large as possible
questions.explanation: At a Nash equilibrium each strategy is a best response to the others, so no one gains from a unilateral change.

questions.prompt: In the classic Prisoner's Dilemma, the equilibrium outcome is that...
options: both players defect even though both would prefer mutual cooperation
one cooperates and one defects forever
questions.explanation: Defect dominates for each player, so both defect - worse for both than mutual cooperation.

questions.prompt: A 'mixed strategy' means a player...
options: chooses among several actions according to fixed probabilities
questions.explanation: A mixed strategy randomizes over actions with set probabilities, as in matching pennies.

questions.prompt: Backward induction is a method for solving...
options: sequential games by reasoning from the last move back to the first
questions.explanation: You start at the end of the game tree and work backward to find each player's optimal move.

questions.prompt: In a second-price sealed-bid auction, a bidder's best strategy is generally to...
questions.explanation: Bidding your true value is a dominant strategy in a second-price auction - a result you will prove later.

questions.prompt: A threat is 'credible' when...
options: carrying it out would actually be in the threatener's interest when the moment comes
it is written in a contract
questions.explanation: Credibility means the player would rationally follow through - the core idea behind subgame-perfect equilibrium.

lessons.title: What game theory is: players, strategies, and payoffs
lessons.grammar_note: Payoffs in a matrix are written as a pair (row player's payoff, column player's payoff) - the row player's number always comes first.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe any strategic situation with three ingredients - players, strategies, and payoffs - read a payoff matrix, and explain what 'strategic interdependence' means. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, why is chess strategic but a lottery is not?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Game theory studies decisions among people whose outcomes depend on each other's choices. A game is fully described by three things. First, the players - the decision makers. Second, each player's strategies - the complete choices available to them. Third, the payoffs - a number for each player at each combination of strategies, capturing how much they like that outcome. We assume players are rational: each tries to maximize their own payoff, and each knows the others are doing the same. The hard part is interdependence: the best strategy for you usually depends on what the others pick, so you must reason about their reasoning. A simultaneous game, where players move at the same time without seeing each other's choice, is shown as a payoff matrix: rows are one player's strategies, columns the other's, and each cell holds the pair of payoffs.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Two shops each choose a Low or High price. The matrix (Row shop's payoff, Column shop's payoff) is:

                 Column: Low     Column: High
  Row: Low          2, 2            5, 1
  Row: High         1, 5            4, 4

Read a cell as an outcome. If Row picks Low and Column picks High, the pair is (5, 1): Row earns 5, Column earns 1. Notice each shop's best move depends on the other's price - that is interdependence. Contrast a lottery: your ticket's outcome does not depend on any rival's strategy, so there is no game to solve. A useful habit before any analysis is to circle, for each player, which choice they prefer in response to each choice of the other; those preferences drive everything that follows.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Use the price matrix above. 1) What payoff pair occurs at (Row High, Column Low)? 2) If Column plays Low, does Row prefer Low or High? 3) If Column plays High, does Row prefer Low or High? 4) Name the three ingredients of any game. 5) True or false: in a simultaneous game a player sees the other's choice before deciding. Answers: 1) (1, 5). 2) Low gives Row 2 versus High's 1, so Low. 3) Low gives Row 5 versus High's 4, so Low. 4) Players, strategies, payoffs. 5) False - moves are made without observing the other.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading the payoff pair in the wrong order - the row player's payoff is always listed first. Mistake: analyzing your own payoffs while ignoring that the other player is optimizing too. Exit: (a) In the pair (5, 1), who earns 5? (b) What makes a situation 'strategic' rather than a solo decision? Answers: the row player; each person's best choice depends on the others' choices.

lessons.title: Dominance and iterated deletion
lessons.grammar_note: 'Strictly dominates' means strictly greater payoff in every case; 'weakly dominates' means at least as good everywhere and strictly better somewhere. Keep the two apart.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Spot a strictly dominated strategy, explain why a rational player never uses one, and simplify a game by iterated deletion of dominated strategies. Warm-up: if one of your options is worse than another no matter what the opponent does, should you ever pick it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Strategy A strictly dominates strategy B for a player if A gives a strictly higher payoff than B against every choice the opponents could make. A rational player never plays a strictly dominated strategy, because something else is always better. This gives a first solution tool. Iterated deletion of strictly dominated strategies: remove a dominated strategy, and in the smaller game some other strategy may now be dominated too; delete that, and repeat. If the process leaves a single strategy for each player, that outcome is the prediction. The logic climbs a ladder of reasoning - 'I won't play a dominated strategy; knowing that, you won't play yours; knowing that, I can drop another,' and so on.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Start with (Row, Column) payoffs:

                 Column: Left   Column: Middle   Column: Right
  Row: Up            4, 0          3, 2             1, 4
  Row: Down          2, 1          2, 1             0, 3

For Row, compare Up and Down: 4 > 2, 3 > 2, 1 > 0. Up beats Down in every column, so Up strictly dominates Down - delete Down. Now Column chooses among Left (0), Middle (2), Right (4), given Row plays Up. Right's 4 beats Middle's 2 and Left's 0, so Right dominates the others for Column. The iterated deletion leaves (Up, Right) with payoff (1, 4). The famous case is the Prisoner's Dilemma, where 'Defect' strictly dominates 'Cooperate' for each player, so deletion drives both to defect.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Use the same three-column matrix. 1) Does Row's Up dominate Down strictly or weakly? 2) After deleting Down, which single column is best for Column? 3) What is the predicted outcome and its payoff pair? 4) Would a rational player ever choose a strictly dominated strategy? 5) In one sentence, what does 'iterated' add to plain deletion? Answers: 1) Strictly - Up wins in every column. 2) Right, worth 4 to Column. 3) (Up, Right), payoff (1, 4). 4) No, by definition something is always better. 5) It repeats: removing one strategy can expose another as dominated, so you keep deleting.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling a strategy dominated when it is only worse sometimes - strict dominance requires it to be worse in every column. Mistake: forgetting to re-check the smaller game after a deletion, so you stop one round too early. Exit: (a) A rational player never plays what kind of strategy? (b) What do you do after deleting one dominated strategy? Answers: a strictly dominated one; re-examine the reduced game for newly dominated strategies and delete again.

lessons.title: Best responses and Nash equilibrium
lessons.grammar_note: A best response is defined against a specific opponent choice; a Nash equilibrium requires the strategies to be mutual best responses at the same time.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compute a player's best response to each opponent strategy and find a Nash equilibrium as a cell where the choices are best responses to each other. Warm-up: if you knew exactly what the other player would do, how would you choose?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A best response is the strategy that gives a player the highest payoff, given a fixed choice by the others. Many games cannot be solved by dominance alone, so we need a broader idea. A Nash equilibrium is a combination of strategies, one per player, in which every player's choice is a best response to the others' choices. Equivalently: no player can raise their own payoff by changing only their own strategy while everyone else stays put. It is a point of no regret and no unilateral improvement - a resting point of mutual expectations. A quick way to find it in a matrix is the best-response method: for each column, underline Row's best payoff; for each row, underline Column's best payoff; any cell with both numbers underlined is a Nash equilibrium.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Consider (Row, Column):

                 Column: Left   Column: Right
  Row: Up            3, 3          0, 2
  Row: Down          2, 0          1, 1

Column plays Left: Row compares Up 3 vs Down 2, so Up is the best response. Column plays Right: Row compares Up 0 vs Down 1, so Down. Now Row plays Up: Column compares Left 3 vs Right 2, so Left. Row plays Down: Column compares Left 0 vs Right 1, so Right. The mutual best responses are (Up, Left) - Row's best reply to Left is Up, and Column's best reply to Up is Left - with payoff (3, 3). Check (Down, Right): Row's best reply to Right is Down, Column's best reply to Down is Right, so (Down, Right) with payoff (1, 1) is also a Nash equilibrium. A single game can have more than one.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Use the matrix above. 1) What is Row's best response to Left? 2) What is Column's best response to Down? 3) Is (Up, Right) a Nash equilibrium? 4) At (Up, Left), can Row gain by switching to Down? 5) How many Nash equilibria does this game have in pure strategies? Answers: 1) Up (3 beats 2). 2) Right (1 beats 0). 3) No - given Up, Column prefers Left, so Column would deviate. 4) No - switching drops Row from 3 to 2. 5) Two: (Up, Left) and (Down, Right).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: declaring a cell an equilibrium because it has the largest total payoff - Nash is about each player's own best response, not the sum. Mistake: checking only one player's incentive to deviate; both must have no profitable unilateral move. Exit: (a) Define a best response in one line. (b) What must be true of every player's strategy at a Nash equilibrium? Answers: the payoff-maximizing choice given the others' fixed choices; each is a best response to the others, so no one gains by deviating alone.

questions.prompt: In a payoff pair written (4, 1), the number 4 belongs to...
questions.explanation: By convention the row player's payoff is listed first.

questions.prompt: Strategy A strictly dominates strategy B when A gives a higher payoff...
options: no matter what the opponents do
questions.explanation: Strict dominance means A beats B against every opponent choice, so B is never worth playing.

questions.prompt: Iterated deletion of strictly dominated strategies works because...
options: removing one dominated strategy can make another strategy dominated in the smaller game
questions.explanation: Each deletion can expose a newly dominated strategy, so the process repeats.

questions.prompt: A Nash equilibrium is a strategy combination where...
options: no player can gain by unilaterally changing strategy
there is a dominant strategy for everyone
questions.explanation: Each strategy is a best response to the others, so no one profits from a solo deviation.

questions.prompt: For the matrix with cells (Up,Left)=(3,3), (Up,Right)=(0,2), (Down,Left)=(2,0), (Down,Right)=(1,1), a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium is...
questions.explanation: (Down, Right) is mutual best response - Row's reply to Right is Down and Column's reply to Down is Right; (Up, Left) is the other.

questions.prompt: A game can have...
options: a Nash equilibrium only if a dominant strategy exists
questions.explanation: Games such as the one above can have two or more pure-strategy equilibria.

lessons.title: Mixed strategies and the indifference principle
lessons.grammar_note: Probabilities in a mixed strategy are non-negative and sum to 1. If a player mixes between two actions, both must earn the same expected payoff against the opponent's mix.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why some games have no equilibrium in pure strategies, and find a mixed-strategy equilibrium using the indifference principle. Warm-up: in a game of matching pennies, why is it a bad idea to always show heads?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Some games have no cell where both players are content - any predictable choice can be exploited. The fix is a mixed strategy: choosing among actions according to probabilities. The key tool is the indifference principle. If a player is willing to randomize between two actions, those actions must give the same expected payoff against the opponent's mix - otherwise the player would just pick the better one. So to find the equilibrium, you choose each player's probabilities to make the other player indifferent. That sounds backward, but it is the trick: your mix is set so the opponent has no reason to lean one way, which is exactly what keeps them randomizing too.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Matching pennies (Row, Column), where Row wants a match and Column wants a mismatch:

                 Column: Heads   Column: Tails
  Row: Heads         1, -1          -1, 1
  Row: Tails        -1, 1           1, -1

No pure pair is stable: whoever is predictable loses. Let Column play Heads with probability q. Row's expected payoff from Heads is (1)q + (-1)(1-q) = 2q - 1; from Tails it is (-1)q + (1)(1-q) = 1 - 2q. Row is indifferent when 2q - 1 = 1 - 2q, giving q = 1/2. By the mirror-image calculation, Row plays Heads with probability 1/2 to keep Column indifferent. The equilibrium is each player mixing 50-50, with expected payoff 0 to each. In a soccer penalty kick, this is why a good kicker aims left and right about equally - any tilt would be read and stopped.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Do the probabilities of a mixed strategy have to add to 1? 2) In matching pennies above, what is Row's expected payoff from Heads if Column plays Heads with probability q? 3) Solve 2q - 1 = 1 - 2q for q. 4) What expected payoff does each player earn at the 50-50 equilibrium? 5) Why can't a player profitably deviate from 50-50 here? Answers: 1) Yes, and each is at least 0. 2) 2q - 1. 3) q = 1/2. 4) 0 each. 5) Because both pure actions already give equal expected payoff, so no switch improves it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: setting your own probabilities to maximize your own immediate payoff instead of to make the opponent indifferent - the indifference condition is about the other player. Mistake: forgetting that probabilities must sum to 1. Exit: (a) What must be equal for a player who is willing to randomize between two actions? (b) In matching pennies, what mix does each player use? Answers: the expected payoffs of those two actions; 50-50.

lessons.title: The Prisoner's Dilemma and the problem of cooperation
lessons.grammar_note: 'Cooperate' and 'Defect' are the standard labels; defection is the individually tempting move, cooperation the jointly better one.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Recognize a Prisoner's Dilemma from its payoffs, explain why individually rational choices lead to a jointly bad outcome, and name real settings that share its structure. Warm-up: can two people each act in their own interest and both end up worse off?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Prisoner's Dilemma is the signature game of game theory. Two players each choose Cooperate or Defect. The payoffs are arranged so that Defect strictly dominates Cooperate for each player - defecting is better whatever the other does - yet if both defect they are worse off than if both had cooperated. The gap between the individually rational outcome (both defect) and the jointly best outcome (both cooperate) is the whole point: rational self-interest can produce a result that everyone dislikes. It is not a paradox; it is a clash between private incentives and collective welfare, and it shows up wherever the temptation to free-ride is strong.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
A standard version (Row, Column), higher is better:

                 Column: Cooperate   Column: Defect
  Row: Cooperate      3, 3               0, 5
  Row: Defect         5, 0               1, 1

Check dominance for Row: against Cooperate, Defect's 5 beats 3; against Defect, Defect's 1 beats 0. So Defect strictly dominates, and by symmetry the same holds for Column. Both defect, landing on (1, 1), even though (3, 3) is available and better for both. Real cousins share this shape: two firms tempted to cut prices, two countries deciding whether to over-fish a shared sea, or teammates deciding whether to slack on a group project. In each, the dominant move degrades the shared outcome. Later lessons show how repetition and reputation can rescue cooperation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Use the matrix above. 1) Against Column's Cooperate, which gives Row more, Cooperate or Defect? 2) Is Defect a dominant strategy for Row? 3) What is the equilibrium outcome and its payoffs? 4) Is that outcome the best available for the pair? 5) Name one real situation with the same structure. Answers: 1) Defect (5 beats 3). 2) Yes, it wins in both columns. 3) (Defect, Defect), payoff (1, 1). 4) No - (Cooperate, Cooperate) at (3, 3) is better for both. 5) For example, two firms deciding whether to undercut each other's prices.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming players will cooperate because it is jointly better - in a one-shot dilemma the dominant move is to defect. Mistake: confusing the dilemma with a coordination problem; here defection dominates, not merely one of several equilibria. Exit: (a) Which strategy strictly dominates in the Prisoner's Dilemma? (b) Why is the equilibrium 'inefficient'? Answers: Defect; both would be better off at mutual cooperation, but neither can reach it alone.

lessons.title: Coordination games and focal points
lessons.grammar_note: In a coordination game the players want to match; the challenge is not conflict of interest but agreeing on which equilibrium to land on.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Identify coordination games with multiple equilibria, distinguish them from the Prisoner's Dilemma, and explain how a focal point helps players coordinate without communicating. Warm-up: if you lose a friend in a crowded station with no phones, where do you go to meet?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: In a coordination game, players do best when their choices match, and there is more than one way to match - so there are several Nash equilibria. Unlike the Prisoner's Dilemma, no strategy dominates; the difficulty is agreeing which equilibrium to choose. A focal point (Schelling's idea) is an option that stands out for reasons outside the payoffs - a landmark, a tradition, a round number - and lets players converge on the same choice even with no communication. The Stag Hunt is a related case: hunting a stag together pays best but requires trust, while hunting hare alone is safe, so players must coordinate on the risky-but-better equilibrium or settle for the safe one.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
A meeting game (Row, Column): both prefer to meet at the same place.

                 Column: Cafe   Column: Library
  Row: Cafe          2, 2          0, 0
  Row: Library       0, 0          1, 1

Both (Cafe, Cafe) and (Library, Library) are Nash equilibria; mismatching pays 0. Nothing in the numbers picks between them, so players lean on a focal point - perhaps 'we always meet at the cafe.' Stag Hunt (Row, Column):

                 Column: Stag   Column: Hare
  Row: Stag          4, 4          0, 3
  Row: Hare          3, 0          3, 3

Here (Stag, Stag) is best for both but risky, while (Hare, Hare) is safe; both are equilibria, and which one occurs depends on mutual trust and expectations.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Use the meeting game. 1) List its two pure-strategy equilibria. 2) What payoff results if the players mismatch? 3) Does either player have a dominant strategy? 4) In the Stag Hunt, which outcome is best for both, and why might players still fail to reach it? 5) What is a focal point, in one line? Answers: 1) (Cafe, Cafe) and (Library, Library). 2) 0 to each. 3) No - each wants to match the other, so it depends on the other's choice. 4) (Stag, Stag) pays 4 each, but it needs trust; fear that the other hunts hare can push both to the safe (Hare, Hare). 5) A choice that stands out and lets players coordinate without communicating.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating a coordination game like a Prisoner's Dilemma - here there is no dominant strategy, and matching, not defecting, is the goal. Mistake: assuming the highest-payoff equilibrium is automatically chosen; risk and expectations can steer players to a safer one. Exit: (a) How many pure equilibria does the meeting game have? (b) What does a focal point provide that the payoffs do not? Answers: two; a shared reason to pick the same equilibrium when the numbers alone cannot break the tie.

questions.prompt: A mixed strategy is needed when...
options: one player has a dominant strategy
no pure-strategy choice is stable because any predictable play can be exploited
questions.explanation: Games like matching pennies have no pure equilibrium, so players randomize.

questions.prompt: The indifference principle says a player who randomizes between two actions must find that those actions give...
options: the same expected payoff against the opponent's mix
questions.explanation: If one action paid more, the player would stop mixing and choose it.

questions.prompt: In matching pennies, the equilibrium mix for each player is...
questions.explanation: Setting q = 1/2 makes the opponent indifferent, so both mix evenly.

questions.prompt: In the Prisoner's Dilemma the dominant strategy for each player is to...
questions.explanation: Defect strictly dominates, so both defect despite mutual cooperation being better.

questions.prompt: A coordination game differs from a Prisoner's Dilemma because...
options: players want to match and there are multiple equilibria
no player has a best response
questions.explanation: Coordination games have several matching equilibria and no dominant strategy.

questions.prompt: A focal point helps players...
options: increase total payoff beyond the equilibrium
select the same equilibrium using a feature outside the payoffs
questions.explanation: A salient landmark, tradition, or number lets players coordinate without communicating.

lessons.title: Sequential games and backward induction
lessons.grammar_note: A sequential game is drawn as a tree: nodes are decision points, branches are actions, and payoffs sit at the leaves as (first mover, second mover).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Represent a game where players move in order as a game tree, and solve it by backward induction - reasoning from the final choices back to the first. Warm-up: to decide your first move well, whose later choices do you need to predict?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: When players move one after another and can see earlier moves, a matrix is the wrong picture; we use a game tree. Each node is a point where a player chooses, each branch is an action, and the payoffs are written at the ends. The solution method is backward induction: start at the last decisions, where the choice is a simple maximization, mark the best action there, then step back one level assuming those future choices, and continue to the first move. The first mover chooses well only by anticipating how the second mover will rationally respond. This 'look forward, reason back' discipline is the sequential analog of finding best responses.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A market entry game. Player 1 (Entrant) chooses In or Out. If Out, payoffs are (0, 5) as (Entrant, Incumbent). If In, Player 2 (Incumbent) chooses Fight or Accommodate: Fight gives (-2, -1), Accommodate gives (2, 2). Solve backward. At the Incumbent's node (reached only if the Entrant is In), compare Fight -1 versus Accommodate 2; the Incumbent prefers Accommodate. So the Entrant, foreseeing Accommodate, compares Out's 0 against In's 2 and chooses In. The backward-induction outcome is (In, Accommodate) with payoff (2, 2). Note the Incumbent might wish to threaten 'I will Fight!' to scare the Entrant off - but that threat is not credible, because fighting is worse for the Incumbent once entry has happened. The next lesson makes this precise.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Use the entry game. 1) What are the Entrant's two initial choices? 2) At the Incumbent's node, which pays more, Fight or Accommodate? 3) Given that, does the Entrant choose In or Out? 4) What is the backward-induction outcome and payoff? 5) In one line, what does backward induction start from? Answers: 1) In or Out. 2) Accommodate (2 beats -1). 3) In (2 beats 0). 4) (In, Accommodate), payoff (2, 2). 5) The last decisions in the tree, then it works backward.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: solving a sequential game as if moves were simultaneous, ignoring that the second mover observes the first. Mistake: letting the first mover assume a future action that the second mover would not actually take. Exit: (a) What picture do we use for sequential games? (b) Where does backward induction begin? Answers: a game tree; at the final decision nodes, reasoning back toward the first move.

lessons.title: Subgame-perfect equilibrium and credible threats
lessons.grammar_note: A subgame is the piece of the tree hanging from a decision node onward. 'Subgame-perfect' means the strategy is a Nash equilibrium in every subgame, not just overall.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why some Nash equilibria rely on threats a player would never carry out, and use subgame-perfect equilibrium to keep only the credible ones. Warm-up: why should you ignore a threat that would hurt the threatener to execute?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sequential games can have Nash equilibria that depend on non-credible threats - plans a player announces but would not rationally follow through on once that point is reached. Subgame-perfect equilibrium fixes this by demanding optimal play in every subgame, that is, from every decision node onward, not merely along the path that actually occurs. Backward induction automatically produces the subgame-perfect equilibrium, because at each node it selects the action that is truly best there. The upshot is a sharp test of credibility: a threat matters only if carrying it out is in the threatener's interest at the moment of truth.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Return to the entry game: Entrant chooses In or Out; if In, Incumbent chooses Fight (-2, -1) or Accommodate (2, 2); Out gives (0, 5). Consider the plan 'Entrant plays Out because the Incumbent will Fight.' This can be dressed up as a Nash equilibrium of the whole game - if the Entrant truly believes Fight is coming, staying Out is a best response. But it is not subgame-perfect: in the subgame after In, Fight pays the Incumbent -1 while Accommodate pays 2, so Fight is not optimal there. The threat to Fight is not credible. The only subgame-perfect equilibrium is (In, Accommodate) with payoff (2, 2). To make a threat credible a player must change the game - for instance by pre-committing to capacity that makes fighting genuinely profitable, so that Fight becomes the real best response.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Use the entry game. 1) In the subgame after In, is Fight optimal for the Incumbent? 2) Is 'Out because Fight is threatened' subgame-perfect? Why or why not? 3) What is the unique subgame-perfect outcome? 4) What would make the Fight threat credible? 5) Define a subgame in one line. Answers: 1) No - Accommodate pays 2 versus Fight's -1. 2) No; it relies on a non-credible threat that fails the every-subgame test. 3) (In, Accommodate), payoff (2, 2). 4) A commitment that makes fighting actually profitable for the Incumbent. 5) The rest of the game starting from a given decision node.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: accepting any Nash equilibrium of a sequential game without checking each subgame, thereby trusting empty threats. Mistake: thinking a commitment is just talk - credibility usually requires actually changing one's own payoffs. Exit: (a) What extra condition does subgame-perfection add beyond Nash? (b) When is a threat credible? Answers: optimal play in every subgame; when executing it is in the threatener's own interest at that point.

lessons.title: Repeated games, reputation, and sustaining cooperation
lessons.grammar_note: In a repeated game a 'strategy' is a rule that maps the history of past play to the next action, such as 'cooperate until the other defects, then punish.'

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how repetition can support cooperation that a one-shot game destroys, describe the grim-trigger strategy, and see why a known final round unravels it. Warm-up: would you cheat a partner you expect to deal with every week?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Playing a Prisoner's Dilemma once forces defection, but playing it over and over changes the incentives. In a repeated game, today's choice can affect how the other player treats you tomorrow, so the shadow of the future can discipline behavior. A grim-trigger strategy cooperates as long as the other has always cooperated, and switches to permanent defection the moment the other cheats. If players value the future enough, the lasting loss from triggering punishment outweighs the one-time gain from defecting, so mutual cooperation becomes a subgame-perfect equilibrium. This is the intuition behind the 'folk theorem': with patient players and an indefinite horizon, many cooperative outcomes can be sustained. The catch is a known last round - with no future to protect, the final round is a one-shot dilemma, so both defect there; anticipating that, they defect in the second-to-last round, and the cooperation unravels backward through the whole finite game.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Take the earlier dilemma, payoffs (Row, Column): (Cooperate, Cooperate) = (3, 3); (Defect, Cooperate) = (5, 0); (Cooperate, Defect) = (0, 5); (Defect, Defect) = (1, 1). Suppose it repeats indefinitely and both use grim trigger. Cooperating each round yields a steady 3 per period. Defecting once grabs 5 today but triggers permanent punishment, dropping the player to 1 every period afterward. If the future is weighted heavily enough, the stream 3, 3, 3, ... beats 5, 1, 1, 1, ..., so cooperation holds. Reputation works the same way: a firm that always honors warranties builds a record that makes customers trust it, and the value of that record deters a short-term rip-off. But in a contract known to end after exactly 10 rounds, backward induction kills cooperation: round 10 is a pure one-shot dilemma (both defect), which makes round 9 effectively final, and so on back to round 1.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one line, what does a grim-trigger strategy do? 2) Per-period, what does steady cooperation pay in the matrix above? 3) What does a one-time defection pay this period, and what afterward under grim trigger? 4) Why does a known final round undo cooperation? 5) How is reputation like repeated play? Answers: 1) Cooperate until the other defects, then defect forever. 2) 3. 3) 5 now, then 1 each following period. 4) The last round has no future to protect, so both defect, and the logic unravels backward to the first round. 5) A track record raises the future cost of cheating today, deterring it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: believing repetition always guarantees cooperation - it requires patient players and, crucially, no commonly known final round. Mistake: assuming a single defection is costless in a repeated game; under trigger strategies it forfeits all future cooperative payoffs. Exit: (a) What makes cooperation sustainable in an indefinitely repeated game? (b) What happens in a repeated game with a known last round? Answers: players valuing the future enough that punishment outweighs the one-shot gain; cooperation unravels by backward induction and both defect throughout.

questions.prompt: Backward induction solves a sequential game by...
options: starting at the final decisions and reasoning back to the first
questions.explanation: You find the optimal action at the last nodes, then step back through the tree.

questions.prompt: In the entry game (Out = (0,5); In then Fight = (-2,-1); In then Accommodate = (2,2)), the backward-induction outcome is...
questions.explanation: The Incumbent prefers Accommodate (2 > -1), so the Entrant enters (2 > 0).

questions.prompt: A non-credible threat is one that...
options: the threatener would not actually carry out when the moment arrives
questions.explanation: Executing it would hurt the threatener, so a rational opponent ignores it.

questions.prompt: Subgame-perfect equilibrium requires optimal play...
options: only when threats are credible by luck
questions.explanation: It strengthens Nash by demanding best responses from every decision node onward.

questions.prompt: A grim-trigger strategy in a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma...
options: cooperates until the other defects, then defects forever
questions.explanation: It rewards cooperation and punishes any defection permanently.

questions.prompt: Cooperation tends to unravel in a repeated game when...
options: there is a commonly known final round
questions.explanation: A known last round is a one-shot dilemma, and backward induction spreads defection to every round.

lessons.title: Applications: auctions, bargaining, and market entry
lessons.grammar_note: In a second-price auction the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid; this pricing rule is what makes truthful bidding a dominant strategy.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Apply the course tools to three classic settings - a second-price auction, a simple bargaining split, and entry deterrence. Warm-up: in an auction where the winner pays the runner-up's bid, is there any reason to shade your bid below your true value?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The same ideas - dominance, best responses, backward induction, commitment - explain real markets. Auctions: in a second-price sealed-bid auction, the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid. Bidding your true value is a dominant strategy: raising your bid above value risks winning at a loss, and lowering it below value only risks losing an auction you would have wanted, without ever lowering the price you pay when you do win. Bargaining: when two parties split a surplus, the outcome hinges on outside options, patience, and who can commit; a take-it-or-leave-it offer analyzed by backward induction gives the proposer power, while alternating offers share it. Market entry and deterrence: an incumbent may try to keep a rival out, but only a credible commitment - not a bare threat - actually deters entry, as the subgame-perfect analysis showed.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Second-price auction: your value for an item is 100. If you bid 100 and the top rival bid is 80, you win and pay 80, a gain of 20. Bidding 120 cannot lower that price, but if a rival bids 110 you would win and pay 110, a loss of 10 - so overbidding only creates downside. Bidding 70 changes nothing when you lose to 80, and if the rival bid were 75 you would forfeit a profitable win. Truthful bidding, 100, dominates. Bargaining, ultimatum form: two people split 10 dollars; Proposer offers a split, Responder accepts or rejects, and rejection gives both 0. By backward induction the Responder accepts any positive amount, so the Proposer can offer a token 1 and keep 9 - first-mover commitment is powerful. Entry deterrence: an incumbent's threat to flood the market only deters a rival if the incumbent has pre-committed capacity that makes fighting its own best response; otherwise, as before, entry occurs and the incumbent accommodates.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In a second-price auction with value 100, what do you pay if you win against a top rival bid of 80? 2) Why is overbidding your value risky there? 3) In the ultimatum game splitting 10 dollars, what does backward induction predict the Proposer offers? 4) Why does the Responder accept a tiny positive offer? 5) What turns an incumbent's threat to fight into a real deterrent? Answers: 1) 80, the second-highest bid. 2) You might win at a price above your value and take a loss. 3) A minimal positive amount, keeping most of the surplus. 4) A positive amount beats the 0 from rejecting. 5) A credible commitment (such as pre-built capacity) that makes fighting the incumbent's own best response.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: shading your bid in a second-price auction - the price you pay is set by others, so truthful bidding is dominant. Mistake: treating an incumbent's threat as a deterrent without checking that fighting is credible. Exit: (a) In a second-price auction, what is the dominant bid? (b) What must back an entry-deterring threat for it to work? Answers: your true value; a genuine commitment that makes carrying out the threat the incumbent's best response.

lessons.title: Capstone: analyze a strategic situation end to end
lessons.grammar_note: A complete analysis names the players, lays out strategies and payoffs, applies the right solution concept, and states the predicted outcome with its reasoning.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Put the whole course together: take a described situation, model it as a game, choose the correct solution concept, and produce a reasoned prediction. Warm-up: given a new scenario, what is the very first question you should ask about it?

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Two competing streaming services, A and B, each simultaneously decide whether to launch a cheap ad-supported tier (Launch) or keep only their paid tier (Hold). Model this as a game: identify the players, their strategies, and their payoffs; find any dominant strategies; locate the Nash equilibria; and state your prediction with the reasoning behind it. Then extend the scenario: suppose instead A must decide first and B observes A's choice before deciding. Redo the analysis as a sequential game with backward induction, and say whether A gains a first-mover advantage.

sections.heading: A worked model to imitate
sections.text:
Use these payoffs (A, B):

                 B: Launch      B: Hold
  A: Launch        3, 3           6, 2
  A: Hold          2, 6           4, 4

Simultaneous analysis. For A against B's Launch: Launch pays 3 versus Hold's 2, so Launch. Against B's Hold: Launch pays 6 versus Hold's 4, so Launch. Launch strictly dominates for A, and by symmetry for B, so the unique Nash equilibrium is (Launch, Launch) at (3, 3) - a Prisoner's Dilemma, since both would prefer (Hold, Hold) at (4, 4) but cannot get there. Sequential version, A first. If A Launches, B's best reply is Launch (3 > 2); if A Holds, B's best reply is Launch (6 > 4). B launches either way, so A compares Launch (3) against Hold (2) and launches. Backward induction gives (Launch, Launch), payoff (3, 3) - moving first gives A no advantage here, because Launch dominates for B regardless. Present your own analysis in this structure: setup, dominance check, equilibrium, prediction, then the sequential extension.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: Check yes to each: you named the players, strategies, and payoffs before analyzing; you tested for dominant strategies explicitly; you found every Nash equilibrium by mutual best response, not by picking the largest total; you stated the predicted outcome and why; for the sequential version you used backward induction from B's decision and judged the first-mover claim on the actual payoffs; and you noted whether the game is a Prisoner's Dilemma, a coordination game, or neither. If all six hold, you have analyzed the game end to end. Closing reflection: which single concept from this course - dominance, Nash equilibrium, mixing, backward induction, credibility, or repetition - did you rely on most, and why?

questions.prompt: The three ingredients that define any game are...
questions.explanation: Every game is specified by its players, their strategies, and the payoffs.

questions.prompt: A rational player will never play a strategy that is...
questions.explanation: A strictly dominated strategy is beaten by another in every case, so it is never chosen.

questions.prompt: At a Nash equilibrium...
options: each player's strategy is a best response to the others
every player has a dominant strategy
questions.explanation: No player can gain by a unilateral change, so each strategy is a best response.

questions.prompt: In matching pennies, the mixed-strategy equilibrium has each player choosing...
options: Heads and Tails with probability 1/2 each
questions.explanation: The 50-50 mix makes the opponent indifferent, sustaining the equilibrium.

questions.prompt: The indifference principle is used to...
options: set each player's probabilities so the opponent is indifferent between actions
questions.explanation: You choose the mix that equalizes the opponent's expected payoffs across their actions.

questions.prompt: The Prisoner's Dilemma is 'inefficient' because...
options: the equilibrium (both defect) is worse for both than mutual cooperation
questions.explanation: Dominant defection leads to an outcome both players like less than cooperating.

questions.prompt: A coordination game is distinguished by...
options: multiple equilibria where players want to match
questions.explanation: Players do best by matching, and several matching equilibria exist.

questions.prompt: A focal point helps players...
options: converge on the same equilibrium using something salient outside the payoffs
questions.explanation: A salient landmark or convention breaks the tie between equilibria without communication.

questions.prompt: Backward induction is applied to...
options: sequential games, from the last move back to the first
questions.explanation: It finds optimal play at the final nodes and reasons backward through the tree.

questions.prompt: A threat is credible only if...
options: carrying it out is in the threatener's own interest at that point
questions.explanation: Subgame-perfection keeps only threats the player would rationally execute.

questions.prompt: In an indefinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, cooperation can be sustained when...
options: players are patient and there is no known final round
defection is dominant every round with certainty
questions.explanation: A heavily weighted future lets punishment outweigh the one-shot gain from defecting.

questions.prompt: In a second-price sealed-bid auction, the dominant strategy is to bid...
questions.explanation: Because the price is the second-highest bid, truthful bidding is dominant.

questions.prompt: In the ultimatum bargaining game over 10 dollars, backward induction predicts the Proposer...
options: offers the Responder a minimal positive amount and keeps most of it
questions.explanation: The Responder accepts any positive amount over 0, so the Proposer keeps nearly all the surplus.

questions.prompt: For an incumbent to deter entry, its threat to fight must be backed by...
options: a genuine commitment that makes fighting its own best response
questions.explanation: Without a credible commitment, fighting is not optimal after entry, so the threat fails.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a game to its lesson?
options: Prisoner's Dilemma - dominant strategy leading to an inefficient equilibrium
questions.explanation: In the Prisoner's Dilemma, Defect strictly dominates and both defecting is worse than cooperating.
